Benjamin Netanyahu holds a narrow lead in the Israeli elections with more than two-thirds of all ballots counted , after Tuesday’s vote saw the highest voter turnout in over two decades.
The prime minister’s bloc was on course to win 56 seats, while his main rival Gadi Eisenkot’s grouping would take 48, based on partial results shared on Wednesday morning.
Those forecasts suggest neither would be able to form a majority in the 120-seat Knesset , leaving the door open to prolonged coalition negotiations.
Donald Trump nevertheless took credit for Netanyahu’s performance, sharing a statement attributed to “Irving C. Schwartz” that said the US president’s endorsement had “turned the tide”.
“When President Trump endorsed Bibi Netanyahu, the whole tide turned, and now, rather than a decisive defeat for a Great Prime Minister, it looks like a big come-from-behind stalemate, or even a WIN for Netanyahu,” the statement read.

Those forecasts suggest neither would be able to form a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, leaving the door open to prolonged coalition negotiations.
Donald Trump nevertheless took credit for Netanyahu’s performance, sharing a statement attributed to “Irving C. Schwartz” that said the US president’s endorsement had “turned the tide”.
“When President Trump endorsed Bibi Netanyahu, the whole tide turned, and now, rather than a decisive defeat for a Great Prime Minister, it looks like a big come-from-behind stalemate, or even a WIN for Netanyahu,” the statement read.
The pro-Netanyahu bloc is now at 54 seats with 72.4 per cent of the ballot boxes counted, as of 10:03am local time (8:03am UK). The Eisenkot-led bloc is on 48.
Israel’s long serving prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival Gadi Eisenkot offered competing claims to lead Israel after Tuesday's election, with votes yet to be counted.
With two thirds of all votes tallied, Netanyahu’s grouping was set to win 56 of the 61 seats needed to form a majority in the Knesset, while Eisenkot would take 48, according to Israeli media.
At present, that leaves both sides short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, and neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot claimed victory.
A deadlock could yet work in Netanyahu’s favour, leaving him in office as a caretaker prime minister during what are likely to be prolonged coalition negotiations or even until another election can be held.
Addressing party faithful at Likud election headquarters in Jerusalem, the prime minister called for the formation of “a strong, right-wing national government.”
But Eisenkot said the public had voted against Netanyahu and urged him to retire from politics, while warning against the use of Israel's security for political purposes.
“Netanyahu is a caretaker prime minister, without a mandate or the people's trust,” Eisenkot said, calling on the security establishment to “stand firm” against any attempt to put political interests ahead of Israel's security.
More than 5.69 million voters, or 77.7 per cent of the eligible voters, cast their ballots on Tuesday, according to Israel's Central Elections Committee.
The turnout marks the highest in more than two decades and around 7 percentage points ‌higher than in 2022.
Serbian police said this morning an unidentified assailant attacked a guard with knives outside the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade and was killed just after midnight.
Interior minister Ivica Dacic said that police were treating the incident as a “terrorist attack” and had raised the terror threat to the highest level and stepped up police presence at key locations.
Dacic said that “a minor, so far unidentified … shouting Allahu Akbar, attacked the member of Gendarmerie and attacked him with two knives".He added that the police officer “liquidated” the assailant in “self-defence” and was lightly wounded.
Dacic said that Serbia’s security agencies had been monitoring the attacker, who he said was a supporter of the Islamic State group. Dacic said that “he kept the black flag in support of the Islamic State on his Instagram” account.
Politicians faced harassment or attacks on election day as millions of people cast their ballots for the pivotal election in Israel.
Knesset candidate Yair Golan was accosted by a man with a knife, the leader of the main left-wing party said.
“Incitement and violence will not intimidate us,” Golan said in a statement and blamed the incident on the “poison machine” of Benjamin Netanyahu.
Two activists of his party were reportedly punched in the face.
Haredi group politician Moti Leitner said he was jeered by a crowd of men at a bus stop and another group approached his home and threatened his children.
Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc is currently leading on 55 out of the 120 seats in the Knesset after more than half of the ballots cast were counted.
The anti-Netanyahu bloc was trailing with 49 seats at 7.40am local time, according to the Central Elections Committee.
More than 5.69 million voters, or 77.7 per cent of the eligible voters, cast their ballots on Tuesday, according to Israel's Central Elections Committee.

articles.title_orig: Xi’s Corruption Purges Upend Hunt for China’s Next Top Leaders
articles.title_zh: Xi’s Corruption Purges Upend Hunt for China’s Next Top Leaders
articles.content_orig:
The fifth plenum comes against a backdrop of years of purges that have had some analysts wondering if the issue is corruption or a lack of loyalty
When Xi Jinping came to power in 2012, he pledged to stamp out corruption all through the ranks of the Communist party. More than a decade later, the pace of investigations has not slowed. Last year, China’s disciplinary authorities opened investigations into more than 1 million people, including more than 100 officials at or above ministerial or provincial level.
As Chinese Communist party (CCP) officials kick off an important meeting this week, discipline – and party loyalty – is high on the agenda. For those who try to read the tea leaves of elite Chinese politics, concern about the apparent lack of discipline is dominating CCP discussions.
The “fifth plenum” began on Monday and is set to focus on “major issues on advancing the party’s full and rigorous self-governance”, according to a Chinese state media. In party-speak, “governance” is a byword for discipline, loyalty and anti-corruption .
As Xi continues to crack down on corruption, the fact that investigations nearly always result in a conviction begs the question over whether targets are truly guilty of corruption, or are they just political rivals to the people in charge.
Kerry Brown, director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London, explained that in Xi’s worldview, which is obsessed with discipline and loyalty, there may not be much difference between the two. “If you’re corrupt, you’re not politically loyal. If you’re politically loyal, you’re not corrupt,” Brown said.
He added that in the CCP system, “corruption is not just material things”, but also “spiritual corruption”, which includes political disloyalty.
Some analysts argue that the reason that the anti-graft drive is so enduring is because corruption is a feature rather than a bug of an authoritarian, top-down political system with a sprawling bureaucracy that governs 1.4 billion people.
Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, said: “Xi has made the party less corrupt and strengthened his control, but he knows that tougher punishment cannot fully resolve the problem of officials putting their own interests ahead of the party’s.
“Xi’s answer is to keep tightening discipline, making anti-corruption a permanent method of governing with no obvious point at which he can declare the job done,” Thomas said.
The job may be never ending, but the plenum is an opportunity to refocus the party’s energy on discipline. The fifth plenum is the fifth of seven gatherings that normally happen in every five-year cycle between CCP congresses. The plenums bring together more than 300 members of the CCP’s Central Committee, the most senior officials in the party hierarchy.
The meeting is particularly significant because it is likely to be the last substantive meeting before next year’s 21st Party Congress, where a new Central Committee will be chosen, and where Xi is expected to be anointed for a fourth term as the head of the CCP.
Eliminating anyone who poses a risk to his authority or to the party’s credibility is a key priority for Xi. And potential threats are everywhere. Nearly 15 years after Xi took office, according to CCP proclamations and a host of recent investigations, the problem is still not stamped out. “It is a deeply ingrained part of [Xi’s] worldview,” said Brown. “Everyone else is corrupt”.
In the past, Xi has warned that the party could “lose its ruling status and inevitably be eliminated by history” if it could not get its house in order. “This is by no means an exaggeration,” he said.
The current focus on party governance comes amid a host of high-profile investigations against senior party and military leaders.
In January, Zhang Youxia , China’s top general and a man second only to Xi in the military hierarchy, was placed under investigation; he was expelled from party last month, having already been removed from the military’s top ruling body, the Central Military Commission (CMC)
A host of other purges means that the CMC, which normally has seven members, has been reduced to just two: Xi and Zhang Shengmin, the CMC’s head of discipline.
Other recent scalps include Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang, and Huang Qifan, the former mayor of Chongqing.
Huang had long been known as the ultimate survivor in Chinese politics because of his connections to the scandals in the early 2010s in which Xi’s political rival, Bo Xilai, the former Party boss for Chongqing, was embroiled in the death of the British businessman Neil Heywood. Bo was ultimately convicted of bribery and embezzlement, for which he is serving a life sentence, but Huang survived. No longer.
Some China analysts have asked whether the recent purges, which have reached the highest echelons of the Party and military ranks, indicate instability in the regime. But Xi likely sees it differently. Corruption investigations demonstrate who is in charge. Plus, Brown added, they are “the most easy and natural tool by which to enforce unity and discipline”.

articles.title_orig: Researchers Propose New Irrigation to Balance Water Conservation, Food security in China
articles.title_zh: Researchers Propose New Irrigation to Balance Water Conservation, Food security in China
articles.content_orig:
A new study shows that China may better balance water conservation, food security and investment returns by adopting more efficient irrigation strategies, and expanding irrigated farmland only where conditions are optimal.
The study, published in the journal Nature Food, was led by researchers at the Institute of Atmospheric Physics (IAP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Hohai University and Xiamen University, in collaboration with several other Chinese and international institutions.
As rising temperatures and droughts put more pressure on food production systems, irrigation is becoming more important for farmers adapting to climate change. But expanding irrigated farmland further burdens already limited water supplies. The researchers therefore look for ways to save water, protect cereal production and improve investment returns all at once.
The team examined 42,190 county-level agricultural statistical records, 3,576 household socioeconomic survey responses and 2,230 irrigation technology comparison trials. It also focused on China's three staple crops: maize, wheat and rice.
The study found that China's agricultural irrigation underwent a significant technological transition between 2010 and 2022. In 2010, earthen-channel water delivery and flood irrigation were still widespread. By 2022, these inefficient practices had declined substantially, while water-saving technologies had become more common. However, the pace of change varied widely across crops and regions.
Wang Jinxia, a professor at Hohai University in east China's Jiangsu Province, said upgrading irrigation and water-saving technologies has long been a key part of China's farmland water conservancy investment.
Wang explained that at the current rate of technology adoption, irrigation water use per area for the three staple crops is projected to fall by only 9.4 percent to 16 percent by 2030. This projected reduction would fall short of the 25.5 percent water-saving target set by the national agricultural sustainable development plan for 2015 to 2030. The plan sets a cap of 373 cubic kilometers on national agricultural irrigation water use by 2030.
The study showed that deploying the most efficient irrigation technologies across all existing irrigated areas could more than meet the water-saving target. However, even such widespread upgrades would not be enough to offset possible crop yield losses caused by future climate change, posing risks to food security.
The researchers therefore proposed a new approach: first improve water-use efficiency in existing irrigated areas, and then, within water resource constraints, use the water saved to convert some rainfed farmland into irrigated farmland. The strategy aims to reduce the adverse effects of future climate change.
The study also found different optimal strategies for the three crops. For maize, the preferred approach is to adopt more advanced irrigation technologies while moderately expanding irrigated areas. For wheat and rice, less expansion is needed, and medium-efficiency water-saving technologies in newly developed irrigated areas could be enough to ensure food security under future climate conditions, meet water-saving policy targets and maximize investment returns.
Zhang Tianyi, a senior scientist at IAP, said the real question policymakers need to answer is which crops need irrigation, where irrigated area should be expanded, by how much, what technologies should be adopted and whether the investments are economically viable.
He noted that previous studies had largely focused on projecting changes in irrigated areas without fully accounting for interactions among irrigation technologies or between existing and newly developed irrigated areas.
"By integrating multi-source data and developing a new analytical framework, the study aims to provide more actionable scientific evidence for these specific investment decisions," he said.
The researchers emphasized that irrigation is not the only solution. Agricultural production is also influenced by crop variety breeding, cultivation management, land management scale and other factors. Irrigation investment should therefore be coordinated with the development of stress-tolerant crop varieties, climate-resilient cultivation practices and the construction of high-standard farmland.
Chen Huang, a researcher from Xiamen University in east China's Fujian Province, said the study drew on three independent datasets collected through different survey and research approaches. Despite their different sources, the model was able to capture the decline in agricultural irrigation water use and the improvement in irrigation productivity in China over the past decade.
"Future research will further incorporate agricultural policy and economic factors such as farmland consolidation and changes in agricultural commodity prices to refine the assessment of irrigation investment," he said. (Xinhua)

articles.title_orig: Asian Stocks Set to Gain on Resurgent AI Optimism: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Asian Stocks Set to Gain on Resurgent AI Optimism: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Global stock markets have climbed as investors continue to bet on bright prospects for the tech giants driving the AI boom.
In the United States, all three major stock indexes rose on Tuesday, led by the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite, which gained 1.18 percent.
The benchmark S&P 500 rose 0.6 percent, while the narrower Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 0.03 percent.
Five of the “Magnificent Seven” tech stocks rose, led by Tesla, up 4.04 percent.
Amazon gained 1.61 percent, while Apple and Alphabet gained 0.93 percent and 0.9 percent, respectively.
Nvidia, the world’s most valuable public company, rose almost 1 percent after announcing a $3bn investment in Meta’s equity offering.
Meta fell 1.64 percent, while Microsoft fell 0.24 percent.
Other big movers in tech included CoreWeave, Western Digital and Advanced Micro Devices, which gained 7.94 percent, 6.95 percent and 5.45 percent, respectively.
Asian stock markets followed Wall Street’s gains on Wednesday.
South Korea’s KOSPI led the pack, with the benchmark index closing up 6.63 percent.
The surge came as South Korea’s SK Hynix, one of the world’s top three memory chip makers, announced blockbuster third-quarter results, with operating profit soaring about 630 percent year-on-year to 83.33 trillion won ($62.4bn).
SK Hynix’s South Korea-listed shares soared 10.89 percent following the results.
In Japan, the benchmark Nikkei 225 ended the day up 1.08 percent, while the TAIEX in Taiwan climbed 2.04 percent.
In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Index was up 0.33 percent shortly before market closing.
“A rally in a host of AI-related stocks including neocloud group CoreWeave, data storage specialist Western Digital and IT solutions provider Super Micro Computing implies that investors aren’t over the AI craze just yet,” Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell in London, told Al Jazeera.
“These types of stocks have become a litmus test for the mood of the market. They typically fall when investors are worried that the AI story might be running out of steam, and they rise when animal spirits are running high around the technological revolution,” Coatsworth said.
“The big unknown is whether this is the start of a new AI stock rally, or just a relief bounce after a period where investors were starting to question how long positive momentum could be sustained,” he added.
Investors are eagerly anticipating upcoming earnings reports from chief tech players as they try to gauge whether their huge investments in AI will pay dividends.
Microsoft and Alphabet report their latest results on Wednesday, followed by Amazon on Thursday and Apple on Monday.
On Monday, AI giant Anthropic filed paperwork for its hotly anticipated IPO, reporting a net loss of $80.7bn in the first half of 2026 on $16.3bn in revenue.
Tech firms have poured hundreds of billions of dollars each into AI infrastructure, prompting debate over whether a speculative market bubble could be forming similar to the one that preceded the 2000 dot-com crash.
Global AI investment is forecast to hit $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to Gartner, a technology insights company.
Oil prices, which have been elevated since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, rose nearly 2 percent percent amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, including hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis.
Futures for Brent crude, the global benchmark, topped $116 a barrel, up more than 60 percent from before the war began.

articles.title_orig: Stock futures are mixed as traders await Fed decision, Big Tech earnings: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures are mixed as traders await Fed decision, Big Tech earnings: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equity futures were mixed early Wednesday as investors await earnings reports from mega-cap technology companies and a rate policy decision from the Federal Reserve due Wednesday.
S&P 500 futures inched higher and Nasdaq-100 futures rose 0.5%. Dow futures were 0.2% lower.
In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 closed 1.08% higher and South Korea's Kospi rose 6.63%. Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 was flat. Mainland China's CSI 300 closed 0.85% higher.
In Tuesday's regular U.S. trading, the major averages ended the session higher . Chip stocks rose again, this time powered by an announcement from Broadcom that a group of banks would provide $63 billion in financing to buy the company's chips and networking solutions to be leased to Anthropic, the company behind Claude. Broadcom rose 4%, while Advanced Micro Devices climbed 5.5% and Micron Technology rose 2.8%.
Those moves led the Nasdaq Composite to rise 1.2% on the session.
Stocks were also supported by lower oil prices, which fell following news that Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei met with the nation's top security official Mohsen Rezaei to discuss conditions for ending the war with the U.S.
On Wednesday, though, focus will turn to domestic monetary policy as the Fed wraps up its two-day policy meeting. The central bank is widely predicted to keep interest rates steady at a target rate range of 3.75% to 4%. Policymakers raised rates by a quarter percentage point at their September meeting .
According to CME's FedWatch tool, there's a roughly 92% chance that the Fed maintains the current interest rate, but some expect that Chairman Kevin Warsh will signal that more hikes are coming in future policy meetings. The decision on interest rates will be announced at 2:00 p.m. ET.
After the bell on Wednesday, though, investors will turn their focus to the AI trade, as "Magnificent Seven" giants Alphabet and Microsoft will kick off Big Tech earnings.
Tech stocks, particularly those with exposure to the AI buildout, have struggled in recent weeks amid questions over the technology's financing . However, Morgan Stanley's chief U.S. equity strategist, Mike Wilson , thinks that the recent recovery in tech stocks is a sign that the trend may be nearing its end.
"Most of the correction is already over," he said in an appearance on CNBC's " Closing Bell " on Tuesday. "We've been in correction mode for four or five months... the market I think has digested this very efficiently."
Japan's Nikkei 225 closed 1.08% higher at 63,954.19,  while the Topix slipped 0.14% at 3,991.71.
South Korea's Kospi rose 6.63% to 6,012.44 and the tech-focused, small-cap Kosdaq advanced 3.69% at 771.28.
Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 ended flat at 8,847.30.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was up 0.24% in its last hour of trade, while mainland China's CSI 300 closed 0.85% higher at 4,083.87.
GSK posted quarterly earnings slightly ahead of forecasts early Wednesday, as the drugmaker continues to advance its pipeline ahead of a looming patent cliff which will see revenue drop for older, best-selling medicines as they come to face generic competition.
Third-quarter sales came in at £8.9 billion ($11.8 billion), up 5% year-on-year in constant exchange rates.
Operating profit in the quarter fell 16%, driven by restructuring charges of £328 million. On an adjusted basis, operating profit grew by 5% to £3.1 billion.
The London-listed company reiterated its full-year guidance and said it remained on track for 2031 sales of more than £40 billion.
On Tuesday, GSK's oncology lead told the Wall Street Journal it would nearly double the number of cancer medicines in its pipeline next year, as Britain's second-largest drugmaker bets big on the unit under CEO Luke Miels.
GSK bought the U.S.-based specialized oncology biotech Nuvalent earlier this year, in its largest acquisition in over a decade.
German luxury car manufacturer Mercedes-Benz reported a slump in third-quarter car sales and cut guidance, citing continued pressure in the Chinese market.
The car maker said Wednesday that third-quarter car sales declined 8% to 407,232 vehicles, with sales in the first nine months of the year down 7% to 1,244,427 units. It cited "intense competition" and a "challenging market environment" in China for the decline.
German premium automakers have struggled with competition from domestic Chinese brands like BYD, Geely, and Xiaomi.
However, it recorded growth in revenue to 30.7 billion euros ($34 billion), while net profit increased to 1.52 billion euros, with higher unit sales in Europe and the U.S. supporting earnings.
"Continued sales growth in Europe and the United States and record BEV sales show that our new models are resonating with customers," Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Källenius said.
"At the same time, market conditions have become even more challenging over the course of the year, particularly in China. Consistent cost discipline and strong contributions from Mercedes-Benz Vans and Mercedes-Benz Financial Services help us counter these headwinds, while our strong balance sheet allows us to keep investing in our future."
The company is guiding for its full-year revenue to come in slightly below expectations, with free cash flow significantly below expectations.
Santander 's reported net profit fell 2.1% year-on-year in the third quarter to 3.43 billion euros ($3.81 billion), while underlying net profit rose 19% to 3.85 billion euros.
Net interest income climbed to 11.83 billion euros, up from 10.35 billion euros a year earlier.
The decline in reported profit stemmed partly from some 416 million euros in restructuring and integration costs related to Santander's acquisition of U.S. lender Webster Bank.
Spain's largest bank reaffirmed its full-year 2026 guidance, including its target for profit to exceed the 14.1 billion euros it earned in 2025.
Deutsche Bank reported a net profit of 1.9 billion euros ($2.11 billion) in the third quarter, a 2% rise year-on-year, while pre-tax profits at the German lender rose 8% year-on-year to 2.6 billion euros.
Assets under management rose by 50 billion euros to 2 trillion euros across the firm's private bank and asset management unit, fueled by record net inflows of 47 billion euros.
Deutsche Bank CEO Christian Sewing said revenue, investment inflows, loans and deposits all grew, with Germany showing stronger momentum, as the bank's return on tangible equity — a measure of how well it turns shareholder funds into profit — rose to 11.5% for the first nine months of 2026.
UBS reported a pre-tax profit of almost $3.6 billion in the third quarter, up 27% year on year, largely in line with consensus forecasts.
The Swiss banking and asset management giant saw strong net inflows into its global wealth management business.
Net profits were $2.7 billion for the third quarter, in line with estimates.
Jio Platforms' shares rose 21.4% on their trading debut Wednesday after a record initial public offering that was lapped up by retail as well as institutional investors.
India's largest telecom and digital services player had offered 270 million shares in the IPO priced at 1,119 rupees apiece, raising 302 billion rupees ($3.2 billion) in the country's largest-ever IPO.
The public issue was subscribed more than 22 times, with institutional investors leading the demand, according to data from the BSE. The qualified institutional portion was subscribed 70.55 times, while retail investors subscribed 2.72 times.
Shares of Chinese toymaker Pop Mart , known for its popular Labubu dolls, added to their more than 30% decline so far this year, following a sharp decline in third-quarter revenue.
Shares were last down under 2%, paring losses after declining more than 6% in early trading Wednesday. They have ended in the red in nine of the past 12 sessions.
The company reported a 45% to 50% year-on-year drop in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to a filing.

articles.title_orig: China Spaceplane CSSHQ: 3 Missions, 8,500 kg [2026]
articles.title_zh: China Spaceplane CSSHQ: 3 Missions, 8,500 kg [2026]
articles.content_orig:
A new Ars Technica report argues that China’s spaceplane cannot hide in low-Earth orbit , and the claim lands at a moment when the program is drawing more public attention than at any point since its first flight in September 2020. The vehicle at the center of the story carries the official name “reusable experimental spacecraft.” Its Chinese name is Chongfu Shiyong Shiyan Hangtian Qi, shortened to CSSHQ.
The headline framing is punchy, but the public record is more modest. The Secure World Foundation describes the CSSHQ as a technology demonstrator and experimental vehicle. Public listings show launches in September 2020, August 2022 and December 2023, with a fourth mission recorded for February 2026. The secrecy implied by the word “top-secret” is something we cannot confirm from the sources we retrieved. That gap between headline and evidence is the real story, and this analysis walks through both sides.
Why does it matter for a hardware audience? Because a reusable vehicle that releases small satellites, flies close to them and comes home is a test bed for sensors, guidance computers, thermal protection and launch integration. It also arrives while commercial launch cadence is climbing fast, as our report on SpaceX tying the California launch record with its 71st Vandenberg flight shows. More traffic in low orbit means more eyes on every object up there, including this one.
Don't miss new tech stories on Google
Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.
Start with the cleanest layer of facts. The Secure World Foundation, a space policy nonprofit, calls the CSSHQ a technology demonstrator. Its assessment says the craft deployed a small satellite during each of its first three missions, and that it performed limited rendezvous and proximity operations with the satellites it released. Those statements form the backbone of everything public about the program.
The mission list is just as plain. Public records place the first three launches in September 2020, August 2022 and December 2023, all on the CZ-2F/T launch vehicle. A search record adds a fourth mission in February 2026. A catalog entry lists an orbit of 332 km by 348 km, inclined 50.20 degrees, for a spacecraft of 8,500 kg.
Now the other layer. Several details that circulate around this story are unconfirmed in the retrieved sources. They include the “top-secret” label, the claim that the vehicle “can’t hide,” and any specific photograph, photographer or commercial satellite imaging event from 2024. Outlets including Ars Technica, TWZ, The Aviationist, Popular Science and Starlust.org have covered the story. The imaging details surfaced in one outlet’s search result, and none of the other retrieved sources confirms them. We treat them as reported claims, not settled fact.
This distinction shapes how a careful reader should handle the China spaceplane story. A craft can be tightly controlled by its operator and still be openly cataloged, because tracking networks log anything that reaches orbit. “Secret” often describes the mission goals, not the existence of the object. That reading fits the evidence far better than the dramatic version.
The acronym CSSHQ comes straight from the Chinese name, Chongfu Shiyong Shiyan Hangtian Qi, which translates as reusable experimental spacecraft. The English phrase matters. It tells you that the program office, at least in public, frames the vehicle as an experiment first. Wikipedia’s entry on the Chinese reusable experimental spacecraft collects the public mission history, and the Secure World Foundation uses the same experimental label.
Press and social media often call it a spaceplane. That shorthand is understandable, since the concept resembles a small winged orbiter that launches on a rocket, spends time in orbit and returns to land. But the fact sheet we rely on does not confirm the vehicle’s dimensions, wing geometry or landing method. We can say that the program describes a reusable spacecraft. We cannot responsibly describe its shape.
What about the owner? The retrieved sources do not name a manufacturer or a formal operator. They also do not state a price, a payload capacity or detailed mission objectives beyond the experimental role. Analysts who fill those blanks are drawing inferences. Some inferences are reasonable, yet none is a documented fact.
For readers who track the broader hardware industry, the naming is a useful clue about intent. A program that stresses reuse is chasing lower cost per flight and faster turnaround, the same pressures driving commercial rockets. A program that stresses experimentation is gathering data, not fielding a service. The CSSHQ sits firmly in the second camp for now.
Four launches over roughly five and a half years is a slow cadence by any standard. The gaps between the first three missions run close to two years, then about sixteen months. The fourth entry, dated February 2026, follows the December 2023 flight by a little over two years. That is arithmetic on public listing dates, not a claim about internal schedules.
Look closely at the fourth row. The verified material confirms the launch vehicle only for the first three missions. It does not confirm whether the February 2026 flight used the same rocket, whether it released a satellite, or whether the vehicle has landed. Any article that states those points as fact goes beyond the evidence we can verify.
That limit matters because the most dramatic claims in circulation attach to the newest flight. Reports of maneuvers and repeated releases deserve attention, and readers should check the outlets directly. Still, a responsible summary separates the three well-documented missions from the one whose details remain thin.
One entry in the Skyrocket space catalog record for the CSSHQ lists an orbit of 332 km by 348 km, with an inclination of 50.20 degrees, for an 8,500 kg spacecraft. Treat it as one catalog entry, not a universal description of every mission. The retrieved material does not say which flight the figures belong to, and orbits change over a mission.
Even so, the numbers carry useful information. A perigee of 332 km and an apogee of 348 km put the craft in a nearly circular orbit, with just 16 km separating the low and high points. The mean altitude works out to 340 km. That is deep in low-Earth orbit, where residual atmosphere drags on any object and where operators need propulsion to hold altitude over long stays.
The last three rows are our own calculations, labeled as such. At a mean radius of about 6,711 km from Earth’s center, standard Kepler math gives a period near 91 minutes. That means roughly 15 to 16 laps around the planet each day. The 50.20 degree inclination means the ground track sweeps latitudes up to about 50 degrees north and south, which covers most of the populated world.
The Ars Technica headline rests on a physical truth that has nothing to do with this one program. Objects in low orbit move fast, cross the sky in minutes and repeat their passes on a predictable schedule. Anyone with the right sensors can log them. Radar networks, telescopes and radio receivers all work on this problem, and low orbits are the easiest to observe because the targets are closest.
An 8,500 kg craft is big. If the catalog mass is right, it outweighs many commercial satellites several times over, and size helps ground trackers. Large objects reflect more sunlight and return stronger radar echoes. Sensor technology on the ground keeps improving too, which we saw in our look at counter-drone tests covering four sensor types , where radar, radio-frequency, optical and acoustic detection each filled different gaps.
The word “hide” still deserves care. A tracker can see that an object exists and where it flies without learning what it does. Orbit data reveals position and maneuvers. It does not reveal payload contents, onboard software or intent. So the headline’s claim and the program’s secrecy can both be par

articles.title_orig: No clear winner in Israel as exit polls suggest rebuke for Netanyahu
articles.title_zh: No clear winner in Israel as exit polls suggest rebuke for Netanyahu
articles.content_orig:
PM's rival Gadi Eisenkot says Israelis voted for change, as polls show neither side has a majority
Read the latest on the Israeli elections here .
It’s the early hours of Wednesday morning in Israel, and the election – one of the most consequential in years – is over. Now begins the real work of counting votes and forming a government.
It’ll take several days to finalize the vote count, but exit polls indicate Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s party has taken a blow – though there’s not yet a clear winner with an outright majority.
Supporters of Israel’s Arab Joint List party celebrated at its election headquarters in Nazareth, with Arab parties projected to gain a record number of seats from Tuesday’s election.
Party leader Yousef Jabareen commended a strong turnout among the community, saying it was “unprecedented and historic in our Arab society.” Arab voters make up about 20% of the Israeli electorate, but have traditionally voted at lower rates than Jewish Israelis.
That voter surge was driven by an urgent desire to dismantle Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition, which includes hardline ministers such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
That sentiment was underscored by chants of “Ben-Gvir, go home” at the Joint List election headquarters.
Jabareen said exit polls showed Arab-led parties can “make a difference.”
He vowed to be a “safety net in the face of crime in our society, a safety net in the face of dangerous racism, a safety net in the face of the demolition of homes and entire villages.”
Context: Entering government could still be tricky for Arab parties. Between them, the Joint List and Raam are projected to secure 17-19 seats in the 120-seat Knessett, their strongest showing in history.
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party is projected to win 21-23 seats.
However, Eisenkot has set conditions for any partner to join his government, including recognizing Israel as a Jewish state and recognizing Hamas as a terrorist organization that must be dismantled, terms most Arab lawmakers are unlikely to accept.
Moreover, two of his opposition allies – Avigdor Lieberman and Naftali Bennett – have ruled out forming a government with the Arab parties altogether.
US President Donald Trump said early Wednesday he hadn’t yet spoken to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, but seemed optimistic about his performance in the election as the vote count is underway.
“I’m hearing that he did very well, and it’s pretty close,” he said, speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.
Just over a week before the polls opened in Israel, Trump called Netanyahu a “Great Warrior Prime Minister” in a Truth Social post , offering his “Complete and Total Endorsement.”
Exit polls so far suggest Netanyahu’s bloc lost its majority in the Knesset – though it is narrowly in the lead over the opposition. Trump suggested that the exit polls might be wrong, however.
“He might be winning, or tied,” he said. “It’s a little bit early, but I’m hearing that in Israel, top people are saying, ‘Wow,’ he did a lot better than people thought.”
The final result could be “a stalemate or a win – but we’ll find out,” he added.
Israel’s elections produced no clear winner Tuesday night, exit polls showed, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival Gadi Eisenkot within reach of the 61 seats needed for a governing majority in the 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.
The three main Israeli TV Channels – 11, 12 and 13 – projected Netanyahu’s bloc at 51-52 seats, marking a steep drop from the 68-seat coalition he led in the outgoing Knesset. His Likud party is still projected to be the largest party, with 25-27 seats.
But Israeli politics is all about building coalitions – not being the biggest party – and Netanyahu’s path to staying in power is now unclear.
Read the full story here .
The release of the exit polls is a key moment that gives the first indications of what the results may be as the polls close. But they are only exit polls, trying to approximate a final result with imperfect information.
And as we saw very early Wednesday morning, they can be wrong.
The initial results projected that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc slightly trailed the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot. But in the ensuing hours, Netanyahu’s bloc either tied or slightly surpassed Eisenkot’s. He also opened up a gap between the two individual parties, with his Likud several seats ahead of Eisenkot’s Yashar.
Crucially, neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot declared outright victory. Both men projected strength and a path forward but stopped short of saying they had won. They simply don’t know if they had.
As the official vote count gets underway, the exit polls become less relevant. Now, the Israeli public is waiting on real results. Those are expected sometime late Wednesday or early Thursday. And it will take several more days to officially certify the results.
So why does anyone pay attention to the exit polls at all? Because they give the first indication of what the results may be. It’s just not always the right results.
As election results began trickling in late Tuesday, Gadi Eisenkot supporters who had gathered at the Yashar party campaign headquarters expressed an openness to aligning with Arab parties to form a government.
For these voters, their desire to unseat Netanyahu outweighs anything else.
Among them were Yigal and Racheli Raz, who emphasized their vote for Eisenkot was a vote for change.
“We are sure that Gadi will do what will be the best for our country, and if it will be that we connect with the Arabs, so that’s it,” Yigal said.
Racheli said co-operation with Arab parties was “not a deal breaker” if it meant Israel could have a new government. “We have to make a change in Israel, we have to,” she said. “We can’t stand it any more.”
“We will prefer that he will connect with other Zionist parties, but if it doesn’t succeed, there is always another option, and that option will be to somehow to connect with the Arab parties and to make change,” Yigal said, adding: “What we are saying is that we trust Gadi, that he will do what’s the best for our country.”
For context: Neither Netanyahu’s right wing bloc or the Eisenkot-led opposition bloc can reach a 61-seat majority on their own. Meanwhile, Arab parties, are forecast to win a record 19 seats according to exit polls. Netanyahu’s bloc will not cooperate with the Arab parties; several figures in the opposition bloc have also ruled out cooperation.
Exit polls from Israel’s three main pollsters shifted slightly toward Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, putting him tied with or slightly ahead of the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot.
Israel’s Channel 12 News put Netanyahu’s bloc of right-wing and ultra-Orthodox parties at 52 seats, according to its latest update to the exit polls, while the Eisenkot-led bloc dropped to 49 seats. The Arab parties strengthened by one to 19 seats.
The poll also suggested Netanyahu’s Likud party opened up a lead over Eisenkot’s Yashar party, 27 seats to 21 seats.
But Netanyahu is still well short of a majority of 61 seats needed to declare victory, the exit poll still indicated. Eisenkot is also short of an outright majority, needing to cooperate with the Arab parties in order to oust Israel’s longest-serving leader.
Both Channel 13 and Channel 11 News found in their exit polls that the Netanyahu bloc was tied with Eisenkot’s bloc at 51 seats apiece. The Arab parties held 18 seats, the polls indicated.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu thanked many of his supporters in his speech early Wednesday, among whom he counted US President Donald Trump and God.
“Together with our great friend President Trump, we are determined to eliminate this threat once and for all,” he said, referring to Iran and the ongoing war.
He also thanked members of his Likud party, other government and coalition partners, his wife and children, and Israel’s soldiers.

articles.title_orig: A US cruise ship ends a global voyage in Asia due to fuel costs and 200 passengers lose their homes
articles.title_zh: A US cruise ship ends a global voyage in Asia due to fuel costs and 200 passengers lose their homes
articles.content_orig:
Company says extraordinary fuel costs have made its current operating model extremely challenging
FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. , Oct. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Villa Vie Residences today announced that it has suspended operations in Cambodia as the company works to address extraordinary increases in fuel costs and evaluate restructuring and recapitalization alternatives.
Fuel costs have risen sharply in the regions where the company has been operating. On an equivalent per-cabin basis, monthly fuel expense that historically averaged approximately $1,800 has recently reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia. The company cannot simply pass increases of that scale on to residents, and the resulting shortfall has placed its current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure.
The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements. Villa Vie Residences recognizes that this is a difficult and disruptive period for residents, crew members, and employees, and is working to support those affected as plans develop.
"Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port. Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses. Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees while we work toward restructuring and recapitalization over the next 60 days. That work is ongoing, and no outcome is assured."
Villa Vie Residences continues to evaluate potential paths forward, but no financing or transaction has been finalized.
The company will provide further updates as material developments occur.

Villa Vie Residences offers a new model of global living at sea, combining the freedom of world travel with the comforts of home. Through long-term voyage experiences and residential ownership opportunities, Villa Vie empowers travelers to explore the world without compromise.

articles.title_orig: King acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins
articles.title_zh: King acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins
articles.content_orig:
King Charles III has begun his tour of the Caribbean by acknowledging the "great suffering of the past" as he faced calls for slavery reparations.
Speaking an event in the Bahamas celebrating local youth, the King said the country's culture was "born out of darkness", and it was "only right" to acknowledge historic injustices.
His nine-day tour will culminate in the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), where the King has confirmed leaders will discuss the region's legacy of slavery.
The visit, his first as monarch, comes in the wake of renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit.
Prior to the trip, Buckingham Palace said the King would not shy away from "colonial legacy" and the impact of the slave trade during his visit but, in line with the UK government position, he will not apologise for Britain's role in the slave trade or offer reparations.
Upon his arrival on Tuesday, the King met Governor General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and its Prime Minister Philip Edward Davis, before speaking with members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force as he inspected a guard of honour.
King Charles, wearing sunglasses and a grey suit, was then met with cheers as he arrived for his first engagement at a youth rally at Clifford Park - where he attended  independence celebrations for the Bahamas as Prince of Wales in 1973.
The young people in the crowd had been given time off school for the event. "It's my first time seeing him in person out of TikTok so he's out there, it's cool," one student told the BBC.
A small group of protestors gathered close to the rally shouting "pay us what you owe us" and "return artefacts you've stolen."
The group of around a dozen protestors was kept outside the main venue as they called on the King to help change the UK government's position on apologising and offering reparations.
"He's a man of influence. The Crown still has influence. And if they do not do it then we will become a republic and we will turn our backs on England if you do not show respect to the former colonies," said one protestor, Sharon Purcer-Cooper.
During his speech in Nassau, the King acknowledged his 50-year-long commitment to fighting climate change and highlighted the challenges faced by low-lying Caribbean islands, saying that "our world cries out for healing".
He went on to call on young people at the rally to "take up the sacred task to play your part" as "in years to come, this will be surely be the measure of every person - how they answered the call to care for planet earth - the source of our life, our prosperity and our security".
The King resumes engagements in the Bahamas on Wednesday, where he will hear how vulnerable the low lying islands of the Caribbean are to climate change.
He will also learn more about the Bahamian tradition of Junkanoo - a cultural festival and street parade.
Buckingham Palace said opportunities for the King to reflect on the legacy of the slave trade will be built into the schedule of his nine-day tour of three Caribbean countries with visits planned to memorials and other places of reflection and remembrance.
A spokesperson for the palace told the BBC that the King's programme on the tour "will primarily focus on shining a light on the many modern partnerships and opportunities for the future", specifically those which are "having a transformative effect on the region".
For the King, the spokesperson added, the "tour is both a new journey but also the continuance of a lifelong one, in which he has sought to engage, understand and educate about the most shameful aspects of our past".
Those themes will be reflected by the King through the nine-day visit, the palace said.
The visit has been planned alongside the governments of the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda with an emphasis on honouring the past but also looking forward to the ambition and possibility for future generations.
The King will move to Guyana later this week where his engagements will focus on the environment and biodiversity.
He will then visit Antigua and Barbuda, where he will be joined by Queen Camilla, for the CHOGM and his keynote speech as leader of the Commonwealth.
The biennial summit will bring together leaders of 56 Commonwealth countries to address shared challenges and advance cooperation.

articles.title_orig: It can be lonely at the top. And that’s just how China’s leader likes it
articles.title_zh: It can be lonely at the top. And that’s just how China’s leader likes it
articles.content_orig:
Last week Beijing’s deputy mayor was meeting with Walmart CEO John Furner and encouraging American companies to invest in the Chinese capital. Now he has vanished from public life, the latest to be swept up in an anti-corruption campaign that has ensnared a galaxy of China’s talent: a former top judge, a spy chief, dozens of military generals – and even officials tasked with rooting out graft in the People’s Republic.
In hushed tones across China party officials are wondering who is next, as the purge continues to reach into the highest echelons of the ruling Communist Party and has even toppled those seen as being close to leader Xi Jinping.
The only person who doesn’t need to worry about his future is Xi himself.
Unlike US President Donald Trump , who is currently battling to save his party’s fortunes at the midterm elections and is constitutionally barred from serving more than two terms, Xi’s rule over the aspiring superpower and world’s second-biggest economy has never looked more secure.
He will take that confidence into a high-level closed-door meeting of more than 200 of the party elite in Beijing this week that is all set to further boost his authority – and his signature anti-corruption drive. Attendance at this meeting will be at a historic low – because of the anti-corruption measure.
The meeting is being particularly closely watched because it is held just a year before an even more important gathering of Communist Party leadership next fall where Xi is expected to engineer for himself an unprecedented fourth term.
The years-long anti-corruption campaign has ensured there are few, if any, figures or factions who could stand against him.
Since Xi, 73, came to power over 14 years ago millions of rank-and-file officials have been purged. In 2022, Xi called to “turn the blade inward” to investigate those tasked to enforce discipline themselves.
But he’s still not satisfied.
Earlier this year he told party cadres that the corruption problem “remains grave” and warned that there were still many “two-faced people” in the party. The war against graft, he promised, would be a “never-ending struggle.”
In recent months, the speed and scale of the anti-corruption drive have reached levels unseen in decades.
According to official data from the party’s Central Commission of Discipline Inspection (CCDI), between 2012 and 2022, over 500 ministerial-level officials have been probed, later convicted, removed from their posts, and expelled from the party for corruption.
In just the past three years, more than 410 officials have been purged.
Some of those purges have reached places that were once considered untouchable.
The party’s top military decision-making body, the usually seven-member Central Military Commission is now down to only two members – one of those being Xi himself . The 24-member politburo - the party’s top echelon - is down to only 21 members.
Over the past three weeks, ahead of the Beijing meeting, the CCDI has been sending out near daily updates of arrests, new probes and expulsions from the party.
The news that Huang Qifan was being probed sent shockwaves through political circles.
Huang was a longtime mayor of the megacity of Chongqing, known as a consummate political survivor who had served under six different secretaries of the Communist Party – and seen two of them go to jail, including a former rival of Xi.
In retirement, Huang was prolific at conferences and on TV, giving his takes on the Chinese economy.
Since his downfall, those who knew Huang have rushed to scrub all mention of their former well-connected friend and colleague from their social media accounts – a common practice in China.
For Beijing deputy mayor Xia Linmao, the purge came suddenly. Only days before, state TV showed him at a meeting with Walmart’s Furner and a slew of other US executives, nodding and taking his notes as his boss invited the group to do more business in Beijing.
Others simply vanished from public view, with news of their investigation not appearing for months, like Ma Xingrui, an aerospace engineer turned senior party official who once ran the vast western region of Xinjiang. The authorities announced an investigation into him in April – after he had not been seen in public for five months.
Being officially investigated for corruption almost always spells the end of a political career in China, with guilty officials kept from the public eye even after they have served their sentences.
And in recent months, authorities have shown they are willing to use capital punishment to enforce the party line, even for those who were once trusted aides of Xi.
In May, two former defense ministers, Wei Fenghe and Li Shangfu were given suspended death sentences, with a two-year reprieve , after being convicted of bribery.
Years of purging has left a generation of younger officials with fewer seniors left who can provide patronage, protection and career advancement, and the situation where the most powerful person in China does not have an apparent heir , in a break from his predecessors.
And for some, that’s just fine.
Deng Yuwen, a former deputy editor of the Study Times, the official publication of the party’s top training institute, told CNN that “now younger people all listen to Xi, isn’t this better? At this point, I don’t think Xi needs to worry about whether someone is already his trusted aides. “
“Whoever he promotes will become his loyalist,” said Deng. “And he has enough time to make someone his trusted loyalists.”

articles.title_orig: China rushes to shore up struggling markets
articles.title_zh: China rushes to shore up struggling markets
articles.content_orig:
Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boom
Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.
The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.
The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg.
AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market.
The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.
The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit.
The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.
“This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand.
The US has banned humanoid robots from China , citing national security risks, and is thought to be considering a ban on Chinese components in data centres. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home.
As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce.
But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.
Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August.
“It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang. Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said.
China’s government wants local investors to invest their money domestically. China has in recent months restricted overseas investment, with more regulations taking effect from 1 December, but these moves have not led to greater investment in the Chinese markets.
Wang added that there was still optimism in other technology sectors, such as AI research and satellites, the latter because their links to the military indicates long term state support for the sector. And globally the AI boom is expected to last for at least another year.
On Monday, US AI company Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude, filed paperwork ahead of a planned IPO that could be the biggest stock market debuts of all time. The company is expected to bring in as much as $100bn.
China has no such blockbuster IPOs on the horizon. And despite pressure on policymakers to introduce stimulus measures to boost investment, none are expected to be announced during a politically sensitive period in China.
This week the top officials in the Chinese Communist party are gathering for the fifth plenum , an important meeting that will lay the groundwork for next year’s 21st Party Congress. The Congress is expected to anoint Xi Jinping, China’s leader, for a fourth term. There is no appetite for risky or potentially destabilising policy measures before then, even if there is a chance they could boost the economy.
Any stimulus measure would be “high risk”, Wang said. “What if it doesn’t work out? Then whoever came up with that policy, that guy would be held accountable”.

articles.title_orig: Why Is Halloween Candy So Expensive?
articles.title_zh: Why Is Halloween Candy So Expensive?
articles.content_orig:
GREENWOOD, Neb. (KLKN) – With Halloween just days away, the search for savings is very much active.
At Nebraska’s largest candy outlet, Baker’s Candies , one expert showed Channel 8 the ‘spooky-season’ sales.
“Historically, Halloween candy will discount as much as 50 or maybe even 60% as you lead right up to the holiday and immediately following,” said Todd Baker.
Baker is the CEO of Baker’s Candies and knows about sweet treats and sweet trends.
His father started the business in 1986, and now Todd runs it along with his brother.
Baker says Halloween and Easter are traditionally the two largest candy holidays by volume, but after COVID and historically high cocoa prices last year, customers gravitated towards value instead of gourmet style sweets, like chocolate.
“Because chocolate is about the most expensive ingredient you can put in Halloween candy,” said Baker.
He says cocoa prices have since dropped, but everybody is still looking for value.
“So you’re going to see a lot of candy in the Halloween pails that’s not chocolate,” said Baker.
Instead, he said you’ll see a variety of combos like chocolate covered marshmallows or peanuts or items without any chocolate at all.
At Baker’s, they have an entire selection of candies arranged by the decade it debuted.
“It runs all the way from the 1920s to the 1990s. Candy from your childhood, circus peanuts for instance, 1923,” said Baker.
And although the Baker family is partial to chocolate…
“I will tell you, if you’re looking for value, the best bang for your buck this year is going to be on the sugar side, where prices have stayed historically competitive and where we still see a lot of value,” said Baker.
He also adds that during Halloween, shoppers are usually buying candy for small kids and/or strangers, which is one of the reasons fun-sized items were created.
But when purchasing chocolate for mor intimate holidays like Christmas or Mother’s Day, people will spend a little extra on gourmet; something his workers are already preparing for.

articles.title_orig: RAF Fairford Incident Was Coordinated By Man Acting for Iran, UK Prosecutors Say
articles.title_zh: RAF Fairford Incident Was Coordinated By Man Acting for Iran, UK Prosecutors Say
articles.content_orig:
London — Two men have been charged with serious security offenses in Britain after being arrested in connection with the incident last month near RAF Fairford, the air base in England that had been used by the U.S. military to launch strikes on Iran, the U.K. Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said Tuesday.
Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, both British nationals and London residents, were charged under the 2023 National Security Act.
Abdulkarim was charged with "assisting a foreign intelligence service" in September and "engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out U.K.-related activities."
The CPS said Essghir was charged with a national security offense after he "approached or was in the vicinity of a prohibited place and his conduct was for a purpose that he knew, or having regards to other matters known to him ought reasonably to have known, was prejudicial to the safety or interests of the United Kingdom."
Both men were arrested last week on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service in a suspected plot targeting the Fairford air base in England.
Abdulkarim was arrested by Counter Terror Police under the National Security Act last week, along with another 25-year-old man — a British-Iranian dual national who was released on bail pending further investigation.
Police are still investigating a suspected terror plot against Fairford after five men were initially detained on Sept. 27 near the base in western England. All five of those men were also released on bail, but police said they remained under investigation and would be monitored.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government believes Iran "played a part" in the incident at the base, which prompted the U.S. Air Force to remove all of its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford . The base had been home to U.S. long-range bombers for many years, and it was used during the war with Iran to launch strikes on the Islamic Republic.
Residents of a nearby town were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police and bomb-disposal experts searched the area on Sept. 27. They found gasoline in three vans that had been driven by the five initial suspects, parked close to an entrance to the base, but no explosives.
Iranian officials have said repeatedly that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets. The Iranian Embassy in London, however, said in a previous statement that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.
Police said Tuesday that six men remain free on bail in relation to the incident, four of whom were arrested on Sept. 27 — all U.K. nationals and London residents in their 20s — and two others who were detained subsequently, including the 25-year-old dual U.K.-Iranian national who was detained on Oct. 1.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu, Eisenkot blocs running close, but both shy of majority
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu, Eisenkot blocs running close, but both shy of majority
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that a right-wing government must be formed to ensure Israel’s long-term security, and that it cannot rely on coalitions with Arab parties “that are against our existence”.
He made the comments to supporters at his Likud party headquarters in West Jerusalem on Tuesday, several hours after polls closed in Israel’s legislative election and the early results were being announced.
With more than half of ballots counted , The Times of Israel projected Netanyahu’s bloc to win 56 seats and Gadi Eisenkot’s alliance, 49.
Neither is likely to secure a clear path to a governing majority.
Netanyahu said the “true results” were still one or two days away, while acknowledging that Likud was projected to become the “largest party in Israel”.
Likud was on track to win an estimated 27 seats to 21 for Eisenkot’s Yashar party, according to projections from Israeli Channels 12 and 13, giving Likud a clear lead over all others in the parliament.
Netanyahu also highlighted his achievements since taking office in his current term from 2022, which he sought to build upon.
“We worked wonders that changed the face of the Middle East. We eliminated [Mohammed] Deif, [Ismail] Haniyeh, [Yahya] Sinwar, [Hassan] Nasrallah, [Iranian Supreme Leader Ali] Khamenei,” he said.
“We established security zones deep inside Gaza, in Lebanon, in Syria. We removed an immediate existential threat that hung over us, the danger of immediate destruction. We struck the Iranian regime and brought it to the edge of the abyss. Iran is weaker than ever; Israel is stronger than ever.”
He said Israel had a “historical opportunity” together with United States President Donald Trump “to remove the existential threat of Iran once and for all”.
Alon Pinkas, a former Israeli ambassador who served as consul general of Israel in New York City, said the party that secures the majority of seats may have to seek an uncomfortable coalition deal in order to govern.
But he said opposition voters would not want the bloc to strike a deal with Netanyahu’s coalition.
Marwan Bishara, Al Jazeera’s senior political analyst, says Netanyahu attempted to put on a “brave face” about his party’s prospects during his speech in Jerusalem.
“It’s clear that he’s trying also to project a kind of success that he doesn’t merit. One, because he cannot form a coalition, but two, the idea that he is the largest party in Israel kind of hides the fact that this is the lowest Likud has reached since 2009.”
Political analyst Dan Perry told Al Jazeera that Netanyahu used his speech to “spin the situation as best as he could” after exit polls were released.

articles.title_orig: VCs will make billions on Anthropic’s IPO, but Amazon is set to make much (much) more
articles.title_zh: VCs will make billions on Anthropic’s IPO, but Amazon is set to make much (much) more
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.
Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.
Many investors stand to win big when Anthropic goes public. Stakes held by firms including Menlo Ventures, Sequoia, Sound Ventures, and Spark Capital are expected to return billions .
Yet according to Anthropic’s S-1 , none of those VC firms owns 5%, the threshold for being included in the principal stockholders’ table. That’s highly unusual. In a typical tech IPO, lead venture investors hold double-digit-percentage stakes in the startups they backed. The reason is Anthropic’s size. At its $965 billion private valuation, a 1% stake is worth nearly $10 billion, so, for example, Menlo’s roughly $14 billion position is only about 1.5% of the company, according to recently reported Bloomberg figures.
While the venture firms may lack sizable percentage stakes, Anthropic sold large stakes to strategic partners, companies that are also its business partners. Indeed, Amazon is likely the single largest financial beneficiary of the IPO.
Amazon first backed Anthropic in 2023 with a commitment to invest up to $4 billion in the AI company. Since then, Amazon has poured billions more into Anthropic. Instead of taking stock upfront, Amazon structured much of its investment as convertible notes, a type of debt that converts into shares upon an IPO or sale.
According to the S-1, Amazon holds convertible notes with $6.2 billion in principal outstanding as of June 30. That is Anthropic’s entire debt load. But as Anthropic’s valuation soared across successive funding rounds, the shares those notes will convert into became far more valuable. Amazon’s own filings valued its note holdings at $97.9 billion as of June 30.
As the value of Amazon’s convertible notes surged, Anthropic had to record the growing value of what it owes on its books. It reported the adjustments on its income statement under “change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs,” a line that totaled $72.4 billion for the first half of 2026. The charge is non-cash, meaning no money left the company.
Amazon’s notes could convert into as many as 1.84 billion shares, according to the S-1. But a cap limits Amazon to 12% of Anthropic’s “partially diluted” share count, a figure that counts some shares not yet issued, such as stock options. Amazon can waive the cap. Notes that can’t convert will stay outstanding and convert in later quarters, subject to the same limit.
But the notes are only part of Amazon’s holdings. It further invested $10 billion in nonvoting preferred stock (a type of equity), in the second quarter, according to Amazon’s quarterly report for the period ended June 30. Amazon did this by investing $5 billion in each of Anthropic’s last two funding rounds. Combined with the $8 billion it invested in the notes from 2023 through 2025, that brings Amazon’s total investment to about $18 billion.
Beyond its stock gains, Amazon will also continue to earn significant revenue from Anthropic, which has committed to spend at least $110 billion on AWS over the next 10 years.
Google, too, is set for a major windfall from both the listing and its cloud computing deals with Anthropic. The search giant held about 14% of Anthropic as of early last year, according to court filings that were reported by The New York Times , and has invested more since, including $10 billion in April. (Google was likely diluted in subsequent and massive funding rounds, with PitchBook analyst Harrison Rolfes telling TechCrunch he estimates its current stake at closer to 5.6%.) It has also secured at least $114 billion in cloud commitments from the Anthropic through 2033.
While VCs set for massive paydays have little reason to complain, the S-1 makes it clear that the biggest winners of Anthropic’s IPO may well be tech giants like Amazon, which backed a would-be rival early on and now sell it much of the computing power it runs on.
The S-1 itself warns that some of those cloud providers also build rival AI models and that they may not always want the same things that Anthropic does.

Exports jumped 142.1 per cent in the first nine months of 2026, with computing equipment and integrated circuits making up more than 76 per cent
A booming semiconductor industry is helping drive a surge in trade in Xian, one of China’s ancient capitals, making it the country’s top performer by trade growth among provincial capitals and provincial-level cities for which data is publicly available.
The capital of western China’s Shaanxi province recorded a 115.5 per cent year-on-year surge in trade during the first nine months of 2026. Exports far outpaced imports, climbing 142.1 per cent.
Two product categories drove much of that export growth. Shipments of automatic data processing equipment and parts jumped 388.1 per cent year on year, while integrated circuits rose 251 per cent. Taken together, these categories accounted for 76.5 per cent of total exports.

articles.title_orig: United ‘hijack’ text scare forces plane to turn back
articles.title_zh: United ‘hijack’ text scare forces plane to turn back
articles.content_orig:
LAS VEGAS (KSNV) — A 25-year-old man accused of sending a text message threatening to hijack a passenger jet bound for New Jersey was arrested Saturday night at Harry Reid International Airport after the flight returned safely to Las Vegas.
Federal authorities said Dante Milne was taken into custody after United Flight 1681 turned back to Las Vegas and landed without incident. Las Vegas police said officers responded to the arriving gate after the plane landed safely, and Milne was arrested on charges of making a threat on board a passenger jet.
Air traffic control audio and flight tracking information show the emergency unfolded about 13 minutes after the plane departed Las Vegas, when the pilots switched to a different transponder to signal an in-flight emergency. In air traffic control audio, a pilot said, “The flight attendant saw a text.”
A flight attendant had alerted the cockpit after seeing a passenger texting someone that he was going to hijack the plane. The crew did not confront the passenger during the flight, according to aviation expert Reed Yadon, who said the pilot’s approach was to avoid escalating the situation. “He just said, ‘Let’s do nothing, just observe,’” Yadon said, adding that precautions were taken “to make sure that the cabin, the cabin, the the flight deck is very very secure.”
As the plane returned to Las Vegas, the crew also had to manage a separate safety issue: the aircraft was too heavy to land immediately because it had not burned off enough fuel. In air traffic control audio, the pilot requested to cancel an approach clearance, saying, “We are quite a bit overweight.” The pilot later told controllers, “We are grossly overweight, so try to burn off extra fuel,” and also warned, “We might need the entire runway. We are quite overweight.” Controllers responded that using the full runway was fine.
About 30 minutes after the emergency began, the Boeing 737 landed back in Las Vegas and taxied to the gate. Air traffic control audio indicated law enforcement was arriving at the aircraft shortly afterward, with a controller telling the flight, “I see marshals coming out right now.”
Yadon praised the response by the crew, saying, “I think the crew handled it excellently. I think they could not have done a better job.”
Milne was released on a $10,000 bond and is due in court Tuesday.
